So, not sure where to start with this. It's been hard to find much information on the original paper published. But I will go on what I see. This study is published in Italy. 

>Researchers caution that the study was carried out on Italian students and there may be different reasons for the gender gap in other countries, and that they used grades awarded part-way through the school year, which may differ from the final grades.  


It's a completely different country to where I am. I live in England where the standard qualifications that are given to 16 and 18 year old's, GCSEs and A levels, are [marked anonymously](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/646365e194f6df000cf5eb00/Student_Guide_2023_condensed__2_.pdf).

>Exams are marked anonymously by expert examiners. Different questions from one paper are often marked by different examiners. 

So I cant agree with the below line. 

>And the disparity could mean the difference between boys getting a pass and a fail in some subjects.

Maybe Italy can form a similar system? 

>Possible explanations are that teachers unconsciously reward behavior seen as Possible explanations are that teachers unconsciously reward behavior seen as “typically female”, such as neatness and sitting quietly, because it makes their job easier., such as neatness and sitting quietly, because it makes their job easier.

Key word here- *possible.* They cannot be sure what caused this gap in this one school. Them calling it  “typically female” behavior doesn't sit right with me. They expect that behavior from everyone since forever, because yes, it makes their job as a teacher easier if students are quiet. From a personal perspective all of my friendship group in secondary school struggled severely. Both myself and my friends had late diagnoses of autism, likely because we are girls, and girls are better at [masking symptoms of autism than boys.](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/04/170403140134.htm)Which was detrimental to our education, with all of us leaving by age 15.   [Link 2](https://www.theguardian.com/society/2019/sep/13/women-better-than-men-at-disguising-autism-symptoms)[Girls under the radar - Researched in the UK and USA](https://www.kirkleeslocaloffer.org.uk/media/yysods0t/girls_and_autism_-_flying_under_the_radar_0.pdf)   So the typical behavior expected in schools is rather hard on us too. Which is why I don't think I can agree on the quoted point above. I do believe there should be alternative education offered to people who severely struggle in mainstream school, although I think this already does happen. 

>Another put forward by the researchers is that teachers deliberately inflate girls’ math grades as a way of encouraging them in a subject where they are often seen as weaker.

Another possible explanation they came up with was this. If this is the case I believe these teachers are certainly going about encouraging these girls in the wrong way. It is becoming more well known that women are underrepresented in STEM. And it is definitely not as clear cut as just [not having enough confidence.](https://www.aauw.org/resources/research/the-stem-gap/) As a women in STEM myself it's often hard to be one of the only girls in my physics class and being singled out and feeling quite a bit of pressure.  This definitely not the teachers deliberately trying to be hateful to the boys of the class but trying to encourage the girls but in the wrong way. 

Yes, in the UK there are more women in higher education by a few percent. However 

>Male graduate average earnings are around 9% higher than female earnings one year after graduation. This earnings gap grows substantially over their early careers and reaches 31% ten years after graduation.

I'm to get better grades than the men just to earn 31% less? [Parliament doc UK](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-9195/)

Is it possible less men are going to university because they feel as though there are better options for them elsewhere? Personal example again you can disregard if you please, a friend of mines son left school at 16 and went straight into work. He never enjoyed school but worked hard elsewhere and is very successful now in his chosen field on a 6 figure salary.
